title: Before and after
job: Time clauses: while, until, since, already, not yet
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE CONNECTIVE FIXES THE CLAUSE, THE SENTENCE FIXES THE TENSE. -gi jeon-e keeps its plain stem in a past sentence and -(eu)n hu-e keeps its past modifier in a future one. Korean marks tense once, at the very end.

-(eu)l ttae IS A TIME, L3-M4's -(eu)myeon IS A CONDITION. English when is both, which is why they are taught against each other. If the clause could take if, it is -(eu)myeon and this module never rewrites it.
-(eu)myeonseo NEEDS ONE PERSON DOING BOTH THINGS, and is written attached to the stem. -neun dongan does not, and is the one you use when somebody else was doing something.
ajik IS BOTH still AND not yet. One Korean word, two English ones, and the polarity of the clause is the whole switch: ajik an haesseoyo is not yet, ajik haeyo is still doing it.
beolsseo TAKES A PAST. It reports that the thing is over sooner than expected, so it sits with -eosseoyo and not with a present.
UNTIL SPLITS. A clause takes -(eu)l ttae-kkaji; a noun reuses L2-M4's -kkaji unchanged, as in hakgyo-kkaji. The bound noun ttae is what lets the particle attach to a whole clause.
SINCE IS A DURATION, NOT A POINT. V-(eu)n ji + a Sino number + nyeon + dwaesseoyo says how much time has piled up. English starts at the event; Korean measures the gap.
THE AFTER-CLAUSE RIDES THE PAST MODIFIER: gan hu-e, on hu-e, meogeun hu-e, bon hu-e. It is never built on hada here, because L1-M8 already owns han as the native number one.

sentences.cue: I wash my hands before eating.

words.note: A bound noun plus L1-M4's -e. It takes the plain -gi stem in front of it and never a tense: meokgi jeon-e is before eating in any tense the sentence ends in.
L2-M5's son with the object particle. Korean leaves the owner out: whose hands is obvious, so my never appears.
From ssitda. The stem takes -eoyo, and the past is ssiseosseoyo.

sentences.trap: Do not put the past on the clause. Even in a past sentence it stays meokgi jeon-e — meogeotgi jeon-e is not a shape Korean has.
sentences.sound: BA-beul MEOK-gi JEO-ne SO-neul SSI-seo-yo. The final -k of meok runs into the g of -gi.

variations.cue: I washed my hands before eating.
variations.changed: the sentence is past; the clause has not moved

variations.cue: I drink coffee before going to school.
variations.changed: a different verb in the before-clause

mistake.why: English agrees the tense of both halves, so a learner pushes the past into the clause. -gi jeon-e has no tense slot at all; the past belongs only on ssiseosseoyo.

sentences.usage: Ordinary household talk, and the line a parent says to a child.
sentences.mnemonic: Before takes the bare stem, always.

sentences.cue: After going to school I met a friend.

words.note: The past modifier of gada and oda. meogeun is L3-M7's and bon is L3-M2's, so those two cells of the paradigm are already taught and are not repeated here.
The mirror of jeon-e, and it takes the PAST modifier -(eu)n even when the sentence is future: gan hu-e jeonhwahalgeyo.

sentences.trap: hu-e never sits on -gi. gagi hu-e is the shape an English speaker builds by symmetry with gagi jeon-e, and Korean does not have it.

variations.cue: After going to school I went home.
variations.changed: a different main clause

variations.cue: After my friend came, we ate.
variations.changed: the other verb of the pair, and a different subject in the clause

mistake.why: -gi belongs to jeon-e alone. After is built on the past modifier, so the pair is not symmetrical the way before and after are in English.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how your day went.

sentences.display: Hangugeo-reul baeul ttae hangsang eumak-eul deureoyo.
sentences.script: 한국어를 배울 때 항상 음악을 들어요.
sentences.cue: When I study Korean I always listen to music.
sentences.literal: Korean-OBJ learn-FUTURE-MODIFIER time always music-OBJ listen

words.note: A bound noun, so it stands after a modifier and never alone. -(eu)l ttae is a TIME; L3-M4's -(eu)myeon is a condition, and English when covers both.
The object form of eumak. The noun is not taught on its own anywhere below, so the particle form is what this row opens; eumak-i is the same noun as a subject.
From deutda, whose d turns into r before a vowel ending. L2-M6's deullyeoyo is the other one: that is a sound reaching you, this is you listening.

sentences.trap: baeumyeon would make it a condition — IF I study Korean. ttae says nothing about whether it happens; it only fixes when.
sentences.sound: HAN-gu-geo-reul BAE-ul TTAE HANG-sang EU-ma-geul DEU-reo-yo. ttae opens with a hard, tense t.

variations.cue: When I meet a friend I am always late.
variations.changed: a different verb in the time clause

variations.cue: When I eat I drink water.
variations.changed: a consonant stem, which takes -eul rather than -l

mistake.why: Grammatical, but it says IF I study Korean — a condition, not a time. The two are one word in English and two in Korean, and choosing by the English is how a habit becomes a hypothesis.

sentences.mnemonic: ttae is a clock, -myeon is a coin toss.

sentences.display: Chingu-ga ilhaneun dongan jeo-neun chaek-eul ilgeosseoyo.
sentences.script: 친구가 일하는 동안 저는 책을 읽었어요.
sentences.cue: While my friend was working I read a book.
sentences.literal: friend-SUBJ work-MODIFIER during I-TOP book-OBJ read

words.note: Takes the -neun modifier and allows TWO different subjects, which is exactly what -(eu)myeonseo forbids. Here the friend works and I read.
From ikda. The written l is silent before a consonant and voiced before the vowel ending, so it is said il-geo-sseo-yo.

sentences.trap: dongan is a stretch, not a point. It cannot mean when I arrived; that is ttae.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga IL-ha-neun DONG-an JEO-neun CHAE-geul IL-geo-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: While my friend was working I drank coffee.
variations.changed: a different main clause

variations.cue: While I work I listen to music.
variations.changed: one subject doing both, which dongan also allows

mistake.display: Chingu-ga ilhaneun ttae jeo-neun chaek-eul ilgeosseoyo.
mistake.script: 친구가 일하는 때 저는 책을 읽었어요.
mistake.why: ttae wants -(eu)l in front of it and marks a point; a stretch of time somebody else filled is dongan. The two are not interchangeable.

sentences.cue: I study while listening to music.

words.note: An ending, so it is written onto the stem with no space. It requires ONE person doing both things at once — the subject of the two halves cannot differ.

sentences.trap: -(eu)myeonseo is not L3-M4's -(eu)myeon with something added. -myeon is if; -myeonseo is while, and only the second one stacks two actions of one person.
sentences.sound: EU-ma-geul DEU-reu-myeon-seo GONG-bu-hae-yo. It runs as one long word.

variations.cue: I work while listening to music.
variations.changed: a different main verb

variations.cue: I watch a film while eating.
variations.changed: a consonant stem, which takes -eumyeonseo

mistake.why: Two subjects. -(eu)myeonseo can only stack two things ONE person does; when somebody else is doing the other thing the clause has to be -neun dongan.

sentences.usage: Saying how you get through homework.

sentences.cue: I will wait here until the class ends.

words.note: ttae plus L2-M4's -kkaji. A noun takes -kkaji on its own — hakgyo-kkaji — but a whole clause needs the bound noun first.
From kkeutnada. The written t assimilates to the following n, so it is said kkeun-nal.

sentences.trap: -kkaji does not come loose. Writing kkeutnal kkaji as two words is the shape English suggests and is not how the particle is written.

variations.cue: I will wait here until my friend comes.
variations.changed: a different clause before ttae

variations.cue: I take the bus as far as the school.
variations.changed: a noun, which takes -kkaji with no ttae at all

mistake.why: A particle is written onto the word in front of it. Split off, kkaji is not a word Korean has.

sentences.mnemonic: Clause needs a ttae to hang -kkaji on.

words.note: Carries surprise: sooner than you expected. It takes a past, so beolsseo sijakhaeyo is not a sentence Korean makes.
From sijakhada. The k meeting h is said as one aspirated sound, si-ja-kae-sseo-yo.

sentences.trap: beolsseo is not the same as English already in I have already eaten as a plain report. It always adds so soon?, and dropping that reading loses the word.
sentences.sound: YEONG-hwa-neun BEOL-sseo SI-ja-kae-sseo-yo. The double s is held.

variations.cue: My friend has already gone home.
variations.changed: a different subject and verb

variations.cue: I have already eaten.
variations.changed: an object in front of beolsseo

mistake.why: already reports something finished, so the verb has to be past. A present after beolsseo leaves the sentence hanging.

sentences.mnemonic: beolsseo always drags a past behind it.

words.note: One word for two English ones, and the polarity picks: ajik an meogeosseoyo is not yet, ajik meogeoyo is still eating. Nothing on ajik itself changes.

sentences.trap: There is no separate word for yet. If you reach for one and add it to ajik, the sentence doubles the same meaning.
sentences.sound: BA-beul A-jik AN MEO-geo-sseo-yo. an is unstressed and leans onto the verb.

variations.cue: I am still eating.
variations.changed: the negative is gone, so the same ajik now means still

variations.cue: I have not read the book yet.
variations.changed: a different verb under the same negative

mistake.why: A past with no negative says I already ate, which is beolsseo's job and the opposite of what was meant. ajik needs the negative to mean not yet.

sentences.usage: Answering have you eaten? — the question Korean asks constantly.
sentences.mnemonic: ajik plus an is not yet; ajik alone is still.

sentences.display: Hanguk-e on ji sip nyeon dwaesseoyo.
sentences.script: 한국에 온 지 십 년 됐어요.
sentences.cue: It has been ten years since I came to Korea.
sentences.literal: Korea-to came-MODIFIER since ten year became

words.note: A bound noun after the past modifier, written with a space in front of it. L4-M5's -(eu)lji, uncertainty, is an ending and is written attached — same syllable, different word.
Counts years and takes the Sino numbers L2-M6 uses for the hour, so sip nyeon is ten years.

sentences.trap: English names a starting point — since 2016. Korean measures the gap and ends with dwaesseoyo, L4-M2's became: ten years HAVE BECOME.
sentences.sound: HAN-gu-ge ON JI SIP NYEON DWAE-sseo-yo.

variations.display: Hanguk-e on ji il nyeon dwaesseoyo.
variations.script: 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요.
variations.cue: It has been a year since I came to Korea.
variations.changed: a different Sino number

variations.display: Hakgyo-e on ji sip nyeon dwaesseoyo.
variations.script: 학교에 온 지 십 년 됐어요.
variations.cue: It has been ten years since I came to this school.
variations.changed: a different place

mistake.display: Hanguk-e on hu-e sip nyeon dwaesseoyo.
mistake.script: 한국에 온 후에 십 년 됐어요.
mistake.why: hu-e orders two events; it cannot carry an elapsed amount. The frame that measures time since is -(eu)n ji, and only ji fits between the modifier and the number.

sentences.usage: Explaining how long you have been somewhere.
sentences.mnemonic: ji counts the gap, not the date.

sentences.cue: I will call when I have time.

words.note: The -(eu)l modifier of L1-M3's isseoyo. Before ttae it is the ordinary shape even when nothing about the future is meant.

sentences.trap: isseumyeon would promise a call only IF time turns up. isseul ttae takes the time for granted and fixes when.

variations.cue: I watch films when I have time.
variations.changed: a habit rather than a promise

variations.cue: I will call if I have time.
variations.changed: the condition, which is L3-M4's -(eu)myeon and a different promise

mistake.why: Half of each pattern. -(eu)myeon is one ending on the stem, and ttae is a bound noun after -(eu)l; mixing them leaves a word that is neither.

sentences.usage: Closing a conversation without fixing a day.

comprehensionPool.cue: I will call before I go home.
I am always late when I meet a friend.
I listen to music while I work.
I read a book while drinking coffee.
I wait until my friend comes.
I have not taken the medicine yet.

comprehensionPool.display: Hanguk-e on ji sip nyeon dwaesseoyo.
comprehensionPool.script: 한국에 온 지 십 년 됐어요.
comprehensionPool.cue: It has been ten years since I came to Korea.
I watch films when I have time.
I meet a friend after going to school.
I study while listening to music.
